publication: The Inadvertent Conception and Late Birth of the Free-Will Problem
position_summary: Bobzien distinguishes a 'one-sided causative' from a 'two-sided potestative' reading of ἐφ' ἡμῖν. The Stoics (Chrysippus) used the phrase in a one-sided causative sense — 'x happens because of us' — meaning the agent is a causal factor, not that alternatives were open. The 'unfortunate custom of translating ἐφ' ἡμῖν by free-will or cognates of free' simply begs the question. ἐφ' ἡμῖν is not equivalent to 'free will' for the early Stoics or Aristotle; it first approaches an indeterminist two-sided concept only in Alexander of Aphrodisias (2nd c. CE).
contested_locus: Chrysippus on fate and what depends on us, via Cicero De fato 40-43; Aulus Gellius NA 7.2
attested_quote: The unfortunate custom of translating the Greek phrase ἐφ' ἡμῖν by 'free-will' or cognates of 'free' simply begs the question.

publication: The Inadvertent Conception and Late Birth of the Free-Will Problem
position_summary: Chrysippus' ἐφ' ἡμῖν is one-sided and causative: if x happens because of me, it does not follow that not-x also depends on me (the alternative is simply absent). Chrysippus used par' hēmas and ex hēmōn in a causative sense (as subclass of what is fated), not as expressing indeterminist power for alternatives. Moral responsibility for Chrysippus is autonomy-based (MR1), not grounded on ability to do otherwise (MR2).
contested_locus: Chrysippus, Περὶ εἱμαρμένης (via Diogenianus in Eusebius, Praep. ev. 6.8); Cicero, De fato 40-43
attested_quote: The early Stoics, in particular Chrysippus, clearly did not have an indeterminist two-sided conception of what depends on us.

publication: Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy
position_summary: In the monograph, Bobzien elaborates the one-sided/two-sided distinction at length. By 'two-sided' she means: if x depends on us, then not-x also depends on us (i.e. the agent has the power for alternatives). This reading is neutral toward determinism/indeterminism when interpreted as a general capacity, but can be read as indeterminist when it implies causally undetermined choice. Chrysippus' eph' hēmin is definitively one-sided causative: it singles out the agent as a cause among causes in a causal network, not as a causally free decision-maker. The early Stoics had no notion of free will.
contested_locus: Chrysippus in Cicero De fato 39-44; Gellius NA 7.2.1-12; Plutarch Stoic. Rep. 1055f-1056a
attested_quote: 'That which depends on us' (in nostra potestate, ἐφ' ἡμῖν) and 'that which happens because of us' (παρ' ἡμᾶς): Chrysippus seems to have understood simply the things (mainly actions) of which we, qua rational beings, are the possible or actual cause.

publication: The Inadvertent Conception and Late Birth of the Free-Will Problem
position_summary: Bobzien documents that autexousion became standard philosophical terminology in the 1st c. CE (Musonius, Epictetus) and that from the late 2nd c. CE it was increasingly used instead of eph' hēmin, superseding it by Nemesius' time (end of 4th c. CE). She treats the Christian adoption as continuous with this broader Hellenistic-Imperial development, not as a distinctly Christian invention. The term autexousion was originally legal/political (denoting self-rule of freed prisoners or divine unchallengeable power) before becoming philosophical. Tertullian rendered it libera arbitrii potestas; Jerome translated it as liberum arbitrium.
contested_locus: Epictetus Diss. II.2.3; IV.1.56, 62, 68, 100; Nemesius, De nat. hom. ch. 39 (on synonymy of eph' hēmin and autexousion)
attested_quote: from the late 2nd century onwards autexousion became more and more common as a philosophical term used instead of eph' hēmin, and at Nemesius' time seems to have superseded it.

publication: The Inadvertent Conception and Late Birth of the Free-Will Problem
position_summary: Bobzien argues that a genuine 'free will problem' (in the sense of the compatibility of causal determinism and freedom to do otherwise) does not arise for Christians in the same way it did for Alexander of Aphrodisias. Christians adopted autexousion from Platonism and Stoicism to assert independence from material causal chains and divine providence. The problem they face is theological (how to reconcile human evil with divine providence/foreknowledge), not physical-causal. No 'free will' in the strict indeterminist sense appears in the Christian sources prior to this theological reformulation.
contested_locus: Origen, De principiis III.1 (Peri autexousiou); Middle-Platonist hypothetical fate theory
attested_quote: If we want to find philosophers who are troubled by a free-will problem within their system, we need to turn to Platonists and Christian thinkers.

publication: The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background
position_summary: Eliasson's methodological stance (following Bobzien 1997/1998a) is that translating ἐφ' ἡμῖν as 'freedom', 'free choice', or 'free will' is a misleading anachronism. He translates consistently with variants of 'depending on' to avoid importing modern conceptions. The various themes labeled 'freedom' in modern scholarship were in antiquity still separate issues (eph' hēmin, eleutheria, autexousion, prohairesis): these must be studied as distinct notions in their own right. The notion of eph' hēmin was not originally discussed in relation to fate (Aristotle) and was not associated with psychological freedom (eleutheria) before the Roman Stoics.
contested_locus: Multiple texts throughout the tradition; Aristotle EN III; Chrysippus; Epictetus
attested_quote: the various themes discussed in the Enneads that we would nowadays—perhaps on instinct rather than deciding from some specific criteria—feel motivated to uniformly label 'freedom', 'free will', etc. were in fact back then still separate issues

publication: The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background
position_summary: Eliasson charts the historical association between eph' hēmin and autexousion as a three-stage process: (1) Epictetus first sees autexousion as closely related to yet distinct from eph' hēmin; (2) Alexander of Aphrodisias first explicitly states that autexousion is what eph' hēmin actually refers to; (3) the two notions become more or less synonymous in later sources (exemplified by Nemesius of Emesa, De nat. hom. ch. 39, where the chapter title treats them as identical). autexousion was established as the standard synonym for liberum arbitrium in philosophical Latin by Jerome, Tertullian, and (indirectly) Augustine.
contested_locus: Epictetus, Diss. II.2.3; Alexander, De fato; Nemesius, De nat. hom. 39 (311.7 ff. Morani)
attested_quote: The Aristotelian Alexander of Aphrodisias is, however, the first one to clearly state that τὸ αὐτεξούσιον is what the notion of τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν actually refers to.

publication: The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background
position_summary: Eliasson emphasizes that autexousion was originally a legal or political notion (status of released prisoners of war; God's unchallengeable power), introduced into philosophical terminology around the 1st c. BCE, and established as common philosophical jargon perhaps by the Roman Stoics Musonius and Epictetus. The scholarly consensus on the date of its first technical philosophical use is disputed: Gauthier-Jolif and Kahn locate it to Epictetus; Bonhöffer and Harl to Musonius; Telfer, Harder-Beutler-Theiler and Zierl to Chrysippus/Zeno (following SVF II.975, which Bobzien 1998a, 355 n.74 challenges).
contested_locus: Hippolytus, Haer. 1.21.2.1 (attributing autexousion to Zeno and Chrysippus = SVF II.975, challenged); Musonius fr. 12 & 16; Epictetus, Diss. II.2.3
attested_quote: originally must have been a legal or political notion that was introduced sometime during the 1st century BC, and that after a while was adopted by philosophers

publication: The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background
position_summary: In Eliasson's section on Nemesius of Emesa (De nat. hom., c. 390-400 CE), Nemesius presents a Christian anthropology grounded in pagan philosophy. The section On That Which Depends on Us (ch. 39) uses eph' hēmin and autexousion interchangeably in the title and text. Nemesius situates eph' hēmin within a standard Middle-Platonist fate account (providence > fate, hypothetical fate) and a taxonomy of modal notions drawn from Aristotle (EN III); he does not explicitly make the identification eph' hēmin = τὰ ἐπίσης ἐνδεχόμενα but implies it.
contested_locus: Nemesius of Emesa, De nat. hom. ch. 39, pp. 109-115 Morani; esp. 311.7 ff.
attested_quote: E.g. in Nemesius of Emesa's NH. ch. 39, including the title as well as the text at 311,7 ff. [these notions appear] to have become more or less synonymous.

publication: The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background
position_summary: Eliasson argues that translating eph' hēmin and its variants as 'freedom', 'free choice', or 'free will' makes it practically impossible to discern differences between distinct notions within the same philosopher or school. The problem is two-layered: (i) different ancient philosophers disagree about which things are eph' hēmin; (ii) the very conception of what philosophical issue the notion involves varies — many writers (especially Stoics) did not even take it to involve moral responsibility at all. Sharples (1983, 9) describes eph' hēmin as used 'both by libertarians and by soft determinists', but Eliasson criticizes this as still too narrow.
contested_locus: Pan-corpus methodological claim, with particular reference to Chrysippus and Epictetus
attested_quote: The most common way of blurring the very issue at stake in a given text is translating or paraphrasing the term ἐφ' ἡμῖν, and its variants as 'freedom', 'free choice', 'free will' etc.

publication: A Free Will: Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought
position_summary: Frede identifies autexousion as a Stoic-derived term, attested twice in Musonius' fragments and then more often in Epictetus. He notes it 'just refers to the ability of a person to do what needs to be done of his own initiative, rather than being made to do it or ordered to do it.' It should not be translated 'having a free will': strictly speaking it denotes the freedom of the person to act as he sees fit in pursuit of the good. Platonists and Peripatetics adopted it, and from Justin Martyr onwards it is very frequent in Christian authors.
contested_locus: Musonius fr. 12 & 16; Epictetus, Diss. II.2.3; IV.1.56, 62, 68, 100; Justin Martyr, 1 Apol. 43-44; Origen, De princ. III.1
attested_quote: Not surprisingly, the term [autexousion] is often translated as if it meant 'having a free will.' But, strictly speaking, it just refers to the ability of a person to do what needs to be done of his own initiative, rather than being made to do it or ordered to do it; it refers to the freedom of the person to act as he sees fit in pursuit of the good.

publication: A Free Will: Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought
position_summary: Frede argues that Christians got their notion of a free will from Platonism and above all from Stoicism. Justin Martyr 'repeatedly uses the technical term autexousion to refer to our freedom'; Tatian coined 'the freedom of the will' (eleutheria tēs prohaireseōs) in the third quarter of the 2nd c. CE — the first person ever to use this expression. Clement of Alexandria still uses the philosophical expression to eph' hēmin. Origen is the first Christian to write in detail and systematically about the free will; his little treatise (De princ. III.1, 'Peri autexousiou') identifies freedom with 'there being things which are up to us (eph' hēmin)' and proceeds 'along standard Stoic lines'. Even Origen's fiercest critics like Methodius found no fault with his views on the free will.
contested_locus: Justin Martyr, 1 Apol. 43-44; Tatian, Oratio ad Graecos 7.1; Origen, De principiis III.1.1-6; Clement of Alexandria
attested_quote: The Christians got their notion of a free will from Platonism and, most of all, from Stoicism. [...] Justin Martyr repeatedly uses the technical term autexousion to refer to our freedom. The first person ever, whether pagan or Christian, to use the expression 'the freedom of the will' (eleutheria tēs prohaireseōs) is Tatian.

publication: A Free Will: Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought
position_summary: Frede notes that Origen's treatment of freedom in De principiis III.1 begins by identifying freedom with 'there being things which are up to us and depends on us (eph' hēmin)'. The explication in III.1.2-3 'proceeds along standard Stoic lines'. Origen titles the treatise 'Peri autexousiou' yet develops it terminologically in terms of eph' hēmin; the systematic account 'could have been taken straight from a late Stoic handbook.' Origen is 'very heavily relying on the late Stoic doctrine of free will.' Crucially, the treatise itself does not demonstrate that freedom (autexousion) requires a free will (prohairesis eleuthera) — for that one must turn to other parts of the De principiis.
contested_locus: Origen, De principiis III.1.1-6 (Greek preserved in Philocalia 21-27; Latin in Rufinus); Epictetus as implied background
attested_quote: Origen begins by pointing out that we shall be judged justly for what we did [...] and that this obviously presupposes that we are free, meaning that it is up to us and depends on us (eph' hēmin) whether or not we do the things which merit praise or vituperation. Origen here simply identifies freedom with there being things which are up to us to do or not to do.

publication: A Free Will: Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought
position_summary: Frede (following his general methodological stance) emphasizes that the ancient phrase eph' hēmin ('what is up to us', 'what depends on us') is not straightforwardly equivalent to 'free will'. The notion of a free will requires in addition: (i) a notion of a will (a faculty by which choices are made), and (ii) a notion of freedom (that the will is not externally or internally compelled). Aristotle 'does not resort to the notion of a free will to account for' ordinary beliefs about action; Aristotle 'did not yet have a notion of a free will'. The Greek term for the relevant notion of freedom is eleutheria (formed by analogy to the political notion of freedom), not eph' hēmin.
contested_locus: Aristotle EN III; Stoic and Platonist traditions; Epictetus
attested_quote: Hence, since even Aristotle does not yet talk of a free will, we should assume that he did not yet have a notion of a free will.

publication: The Hellenistic Philosophers (2 vols.)
position_summary: Long and Sedley note (vol. II, p. 310, in a commentary on Origen's passage on the taxonomy of motion, SVF 53A) that apo (from) was a stronger term for 'personal agency' in Stoic Greek than di' ('through'). They discuss this in the context of distinguishing Stoic expressions for self-caused motion (ex heautōn, aph' hautōn, di' hautōn). This observation is cited by Labarrière (2009) to support a reading of Alexander's use of dia + genitive as a late Aristotelian appropriation of Stoic terminology to specify what he means by to eph' hēmin.
contested_locus: Origen, De oratione VI.1 = SVF II.989; Alexander, De fato XXIV, XXVI; Stoic taxonomy of motion

publication: De 'ce qui dépend de nous'
position_summary: Labarrière (CNRS-Maison française d'Oxford) argues against the tendency to read the ancient eph' hēmin through the lens of modern 'subjectivity', 'liberty', or 'free will'. He resists evolutionist readings that see Greek philosophy as progressing toward modern conceptions. He quotes Gauthier (1970) who located the technical first use of autexousion in Epictetus (1st c. CE) but notes Gauthier did so within a perspective 'strongly marked by Christian literature'. The key point: to autexousion / hē autexousiōtēs ('literally mastery over oneself', earliest technical use in Epictetus 5 times) was only later rendered liberum arbitrium by Jerome (Adv. Pel. III.7); Tertullian's 'hesitations' led him to propose libera arbitrii potestas.
contested_locus: Aristotle EN III.5-7 (seven occurrences of eph' hēmin in eight lines, 1113b7-14); Epictetus; Alexander; Origen
attested_quote: Le mot de 'libre arbitre' n'apparaîtra dans la langue grecque que beaucoup plus tard, en même temps qu'eleutheria prendra le sens de liberté psychologique : ce sera to autexousion (ou hē autexiousiōtēs), littéralement la maîtrise de soi : le plus ancien exemple se trouve dans Diodore de Sicile, 19, 105, 4 (Ier siècle av. J.-C.), mais il n'a pas encore chez lui sa valeur technique ; celle-ci est déjà bien fixée chez Épictète (Ier siècle apr. J.-C.) [citing Gauthier 1970, II.1, p. 217]

publication: De 'ce qui dépend de nous'
position_summary: Labarrière argues that Alexander's De fato mixes Aristotelian (bouleusis, orexis, proairesis, eph' hēmin) and Stoic vocabulary (sunkatathesis, hexis, horme, phantasia, autexousion) not as eclecticism but as deliberate polemic strategy. Alexander 'appropriates new tools forged by the Stoics' in order to turn them against their makers. For Alexander, eph' hēmin requires the possibility of saying 'yes' or 'no' — a two-sided deliberative capacity (bouleusis / proairesis) — which the Stoics' sunkatathesis model (in which agency reduces to responding to impressions) destroys. The Stoics, by restricting eph' hēmin to 'correct use of impressions', eliminate deliberation and treat humans as mere animals. Alexander invokes weakness of 'mortal nature' and accidental causes to ground the proper eph' hēmin.
contested_locus: Alexander, De fato XIV (autexousion / to eph' hēmin identification); Mantissa XXII-XXIII; Origen, De principiis III.1-3 (cited by Labarrière to illuminate Stoic theory of motion)
attested_quote: Ceux qui leur demandent : 'Comment est-il possible, si toutes choses sont selon le destin (panton ontōn kath'heimarmenēn), de sauvegarder ce qui dépend de nous (to eph' hēmin sozesthai) ?' ne demandent pas cela en considérant seulement le mot (onoma) de 'ce qui dépend de nous (tou eph' hēmin)', mais aussi ce qui est signifié (semainomenon) <par> to autexousion (ce qui est notre pouvoir ? libre-arbitre ? liberté ?)

publication: The Inadvertent Conception and Late Birth of the Free-Will Problem
position_summary: Bobzien argues that Aristotle's concept of eph' hēmin does not entail indeterminism. Aristotle uses eph' hēmin in a two-sided sense (if x depends on us, then not-x does too — EN 1113b5-8 is the paradigm passage) but this two-sided reading is 'neutral toward determinism and indeterminism': walking depends on me at a time if I have the general two-sided capacity for walking, even if in the specific situation it is fully causally determined what I will do. The indeterminist reading of a two-sided eph' hēmin is a later development, not Aristotelian.
contested_locus: Aristotle, EN III.5, 1113b5-8; 1135a23-8 (absence of external hindrances)
attested_quote: Aristotle's concept of what depends on us does not entail indeterminism. We have no reason to assume that he has anything more in mind than that the things that depend on us are those which on a generic level it is possible for us to do and not to do, given that we are not externally prevented from doing them.

publication: The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background
position_summary: Eliasson, following Bobzien (1998a, 407), argues that Alexander of Aphrodisias' most significant contribution to the tradition is the replacement of dynasthai ('to be capable of') by exousia ('power/authority') in accounts of eph' hēmin. This shift — from 'having a capacity to act and not act' to 'having authority/control over acting and not acting' — introduces the idea of the agent as a 'causally undetermined decision-maker'. However, Bobzien qualifies that Alexander is 'by no means clear and consistent about whether his phrases like 'having the power to do/choose opposites' are to be understood as indeterminist, although in some places he clearly did.' Eliasson partially disputes Bobzien's explanation for why Alexander made this move.
contested_locus: Alexander, De fato ch. XIV-XV (181.5; 180.26-8); Mantissa ch. 22-23
attested_quote: [Bobzien 1998a, 407] the importance of realising the very different philosophical functions of the terms eleutheria and eph' hemin; Bobzien sees Alexander as using to eph' hemin as meaning that which we not only have the two-sided ability to choose or not to choose, but that which we moreover have the power, authority over choosing or not choosing.

publication: A Free Will: Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought
position_summary: Frede observes a telling terminological shift from Clement to Origen: in Clement of Alexandria (Origen's predecessor in the Alexandrian tradition), 'the discussion is still in terms of that well-worn philosophical expression' to eph' hēmin. Origen, however, titles his treatise 'Peri autexousiou' while using eph' hēmin in the body of III.1.1 to define what freedom is. This duality — autexousion as the title/concept, eph' hēmin as its operational definition — marks the transitional moment in the Greek→Christian semantic shift. Origen treats both as equivalent, but the terminological preference for autexousion indicates assimilation of the term's growing Christian currency.
contested_locus: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata; Origen, De principiis III.1.1 (Peri autexousiou); Philocalia 21-27
attested_quote: the discussion in Clement is still in terms of that well-worn philosophical expression [to eph' hēmin]. [...] At this point we should take a brief look at Origen's short treatise 'On Freedom' (Peri autexousiou) in De princ. III.1.

publication: The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background
position_summary: Eliasson notes that autexousion 'becomes adopted by Christians', citing Methodius of Olympus, Origen, and Hippolytus, with extensive references to the Patristic Greek Lexicon (PGL). This adoption follows the established pagan trajectory (Peripatetics, Stoics, Middle Platonists) and represents continuity with, not departure from, the philosophical tradition. Eliasson does not claim a discontinuous 'Christian invention' of autexousion.
contested_locus: Methodius of Olympus, De autexousio; Origen throughout; Hippolytus
attested_quote: E.g. in Methodius of Olympus; in Origen; in Hippolytus. Cf. the extensive references in PGL.
